data.title: Devín – Great Moravian Dowina above the confluence of the Morava and the Danube
data.excerpt: On a promontory above the confluence of the Morava and the Danube, where the Amber and Danube roads crossed, Devín guarded the crossing of the Danube from the Eastern March and grew into an agglomeration of at least three hillforts. In 864 King Louis the German besieged Rastislav in the town the Annals of Fulda call Dowina — and never even attempted to take its formidable defences by force.
data.metaTitle: Devín – Great Moravian Dowina in the Annals of Fulda
data.metaDescription: Devín, the Dowina where King Louis besieged Rastislav in 864 according to the Annals of Fulda: a site with a dense concentration of archaeological finds.

keyFacts.label: Location
keyFacts.value: A promontory above the confluence of the Danube and the Morava, at the crossing of the Amber and Danube roads

keyFacts.label: The Devín bread
keyFacts.value: A charred round loaf (c. 23 cm in diameter, c. 1 kg) of the Germanic period, baked from wheat flour with an admixture of rye

keyFacts.label: A system of three hillforts
keyFacts.value: The central hillfort (the present-day castle) plus the satellite hillforts of Na pieskoch and Nad lomom on Devínska Kobyla, both with grillage-built defences and traces of a destructive fire

keyFacts.label: The triconch church
keyFacts.value: A three-apse church building of the 9th century, its walls covered with white lime plaster, the interior decorated with paintings

keyFacts.label: Three cemeteries outside the hillfort
keyFacts.value: Mladošovičov vinohrad (13 graves, J. Eisner), Staré Vinohrady (24 graves, 1953, Ľ. Kraskovská) and Za kostolom (122 graves, I. Keller)

keyFacts.label: Written sources
keyFacts.value: The Annals of Fulda and of St Bertin, the Annals of Xanten and the Deeds of the Frankish Kings mention Dowina/Devín in connection with the campaign of Louis the German in 864

keyFacts.label: Access
keyFacts.value: The Na pieskoch and Nad lomom hillforts still carry no tourist signage of any kind about their Great Moravian importance

timeline.title: The earliest occupation of the castle hill
timeline.description: The Linear Pottery culture, the Baden culture, the Corded Ware people and the Maďarovce culture left behind cult artefacts; the people of the Maďarovce culture built the first fortification of the acropolis, a timber-and-earth rampart up to 4 m thick at its base.

timeline.title: Celtic occupation
timeline.description: The find of a jug with 70 Celtic coins (imitations of Roman denarii struck by the Eravisci and the Azali) in the courtyard of the middle castle.

timeline.title: Roman buildings
timeline.description: The Romans built a masonry watchtower on the acropolis and a larger four-room building with an apse in the courtyard of the middle castle, part of the Limes Romanus system.

timeline.title: The first Slavic hillfort
timeline.description: It made use of the remains of the older Roman fortification (the rampart on the northern side); in this period the focus of occupation probably shifted from Devínska Nová Ves to the Devín area.

timeline.title: Devín as an Avar base
timeline.description: According to the historian Ján Steinhübel, the Avars controlled the Slavs in Moravia from here; this is borne out by the increase in horsemen's graves in the surrounding area and by a richly furnished grave of an Avar horseman in the village of Devín itself.

timeline.title: The Moravian princes take possession of Devín
timeline.description: After Avar power had been weakened, the Moravian princes subdued Devín once again and began to rebuild it into one of their most important fortresses.

timeline.title: Rastislav's Devín — the height of its importance
timeline.description: Devín protected the crossing of the Danube from the Eastern March as well as the border against Nitra; the satellite hillforts of Na pieskoch and Nad lomom on Devínska Kobyla arose around the central hillfort.

timeline.title: The siege of Dowina by King Louis the German
timeline.description: The Annals of Fulda record how the Frankish king besieged Rastislav in the town of Dowina; Rastislav finally swore an oath of fealty (which he did not keep) — the defences of Devín proved so imposing that Louis did not even attempt to take them by force.

timeline.title: The discovery of the three-apse church building
timeline.description: The triconch church uncovered at the locality known as “Nad prístaviskom”, built at one time (its walls bonded together) and decorated with painted plaster in the same way as the churches at Mikulčice and at Bratislava Castle.

timeline.title: The cemetery by the church
timeline.description: 6 graves dated to the 9th century survived beside the church building; the later cemetery lying across the walls of the church (11th–13th century) shows that the building was already in ruins.

timeline.title: The excavation of the Staré Vinohrady cemetery
timeline.description: Ľ. Kraskovská uncovered 24 graves, including three symbolic ones (cenotaphs).

timeline.title: The largest cemetery, “Za kostolom”
timeline.description: I. Keller uncovered 122 graves, almost half of them children's graves.

blocks.text: In the month of August King Louis marched out with a great army across the Danube and besieged Rastislav in a certain town which in the tongue of that people is called Dowina. He (Rastislav), however, since he did not dare to meet the king's armies, and since he saw that he had no way by which he might escape, was forced in his straits to give as many hostages, and in such number, as the king commanded. He furthermore confirmed by oath that he, with all his (Rastislav's) magnates, would keep faith with the king for all his days, even though he had not kept it until then.

children.text: The village of Devín is known for its dense concentration of archaeological finds from every archaeological period. As the historian Anton Hrnko puts it in his excellent little book Devín-božská perla Slovenska (Devín – the Divine Pearl of Slovakia), “The uniqueness of the place at the confluence of the Morava with the Danube is heightened by the fact that it was precisely below it that the two most important ancient road routes in Europe crossed, the so-called Amber Road and Danube Road. From the earliest times, below the castle crag and in its surroundings, merchants who handled the exchange trade between northern and southern Europe met those who set out with goods along the Danube from north-western Europe to the Balkans and from there on across Anatolia as far as the Middle East and China, and vice versa. Amber, tin, copper, salt, gold, foodstuffs, cloth and other needed commodities which occurred in one corner of the world were carried to the other end of the trade routes to be exchanged there for other useful things, and travelled along the very same roads, only in the opposite direction.

Today we can only marvel at the enormous distances that ancient merchants were already covering in order to bring the goods that were needed from one part of Europe to another. Then as now, trade needed protection and the upkeep of the trade routes. Strategic places on the busy merchant routes were therefore always fortified, and their inhabitants guarded the roads as far as was necessary and kept them in a usable state. The merchants thus received the protection they needed, and in return left part of their profit to their protectors in the form of various tolls and fees. The benefit was therefore on both sides. If, in addition, several long-distance roads met at a strategic place, the importance of such a point grew considerably. That was also the case with Devín.” He goes on to state that “the earliest inhabitants of the castle hill in the Neolithic (the Linear Pottery culture, the Baden culture, the Corded Ware people and the people of the Maďarovce culture) already left behind artefacts which served cult purposes. During the settlement of the people of the Maďarovce culture the first fortification of the Devín acropolis was also built, a timber-and-earth rampart which reached a thickness of as much as four metres at its base.” A great many finds from later periods have also been made at Devín, which testify to the frequent cult and military use of Devín by many cultures.

blocks.text:
Děvín, dear Děvín, castle left forlorn,
tell us now, when did these ramparts of yours stand?

My ramparts stood in the days of Rastislav:
he was the glory of your fathers, he the glory of my ramparts.

Glory, my glory, where is it you now rest?
Ah, in vain, little wind, do you scatter its dust abroad!

The Celts

blocks.alt: Devín in the time of Prince Rastislav in the 9th century, as imagined by a painter in the 1930s

children.text: Among the first historically known peoples who lived at Devín are, of course, the Celts, who left us a great many interesting finds, among which the find of coins stands out above all. On this important find Hrnko states that a jug containing as many as 70 Celtic coins was found on the remains of the Roman buildings in the courtyard of the middle castle, between the Renaissance palace and the well. The coins were not local, nor were they from the issues then produced by the important Celtic mint in the territory of present-day Bratislava. They belonged among the imitations of Roman denarii struck by the Celtic tribes in Transdanubia with their centre in present-day Budapest – the Eravisci and the Azali. Apart from its numismatic value, what is interesting about the find is that it is not clear who actually put it into the ground. Was it hidden there by a Celtic merchant engaged in long-distance trade who felt under threat? In that case, however, the Romans who were levelling the ground for their building must have been very inattentive – one would say almost blind. Or was it hidden there by some Roman as his booty or his trading profit, who for unknown reasons never came back?
The Germanic peoples

blocks.caption: An early Slavic camp at Devín. Artist: Anton Pinkava, 1937
blocks.alt: An early Slavic camp at Devín. Artist: Anton Pinkava, 1937

children.text: In the period after the turn of the era the territory of present-day Slovakia was occupied by Germanic tribes, above all the Marcomanni and the Quadi. From the time of their stay at Devín we have a documented find that is both very rare and important — ancient bread. The Devín bread was found in the fill of the pit of a destroyed oven, together with several kinds of cereals and further pieces of bread. The circumstances of the find show that it was prepared on the spot from flour which must have been ground from grain somewhere nearby. The round loaf, about 23 cm in diameter and roughly 6.5 cm thick, may have weighed about 1 kg at the time it was baked. According to the analysis it was baked from wheat flour with an admixture of rye flour. The surviving pieces show that, following the Roman practice, the people of the time did not cut the bread but broke the pieces off the loaf by hand. The destruction of the oven and the subsequent charring of the bread and the grain around it probably happened during some violent, unexpected event, most likely during a military capture of the castle hill, which would have been nothing unusual in those restless times. And what might the bread of that time have tasted like? It probably differed little in many respects from today's dark wheat-and-rye breads. If it was well baked, the inhabitants of the castle at that time will certainly have enjoyed it.
The Romans

The Germanic peoples represented a great danger to the Roman Empire, and because of this danger the Roman army built, among other places, a system of fortifications along the course of the Danube known as the Limes Romanus. Already on their first contact with the territory of present-day Slovakia the Romans realised the extraordinary importance of the Devín castle rise, and for that reason they built a masonry watchtower on the acropolis, the foundations of which have been uncovered in the area of the courtyard of the middle castle. 
   Archaeologists have managed to document two larger Roman buildings on the castle hill and one Roman villa in nearby Dúbravka, in the valley on the opposite slope of Devínska Kobyla. The largest building stood in the courtyard of the middle castle, and I have already spoken of it in connection with the find of Celtic coins. It was a building of the 3rd to 4th century consisting of four rooms, one of which ended in an apse. In its layout it resembles a bath house, yet it seems illogical for such a feature to stand on a hill with no direct water supply. Despite a re-examination, the purpose of the building has so far remained open. It is gratifying that after the features were uncovered in the middle of the 1990s, and in spite of the initial financial difficulties, money was eventually found so that they could be presented to visitors to the castle. The second larger Roman feature lies on the northern slope, but we shall speak of it separately.

After the arrival of the Slavs in the territory of present-day Slovakia they naturally settled at Devín and in its surroundings as well. Some historians identify Devín with the legendary Wogastisburg, a subject that is discussed in a separate article. After the death of the ruler Samo the Avars again gained partial control of the territory of present-day Slovakia, although their relationship to the Slavs was no longer as dominant as before the rise of Samo's Empire; it was rather a coexistence with the Slavs, who in the end absorbed the Avars completely. An important Avar base, from which, according to the historian Ján Steinhübel, they controlled the Slavs in Moravia (later the Principality of Moravia), was precisely Devín. Their presence at Devín in this period is documented by the marked increase in horsemen's graves in the cemeteries at Devínska Nová Ves and Záhorská Bystrica, and also by an isolated, richly furnished grave of an Avar horseman in the centre of the village of Devín. According to the same historian, the growth of Avar power at the end of the 7th century was accompanied by a consolidation of the power of the Slavic princes in Moravia and in the Nitra region, which were not directly occupied by the Avars.

blocks.alt: Slavic women graced Devín more than 1,100 years ago

children.text: Hrnko writes that “after the internal strife within the Avar Empire, which culminated in the murder of the khagan in the middle of the 790s, the tudun tried to save himself by going over to the Frankish side. Charlemagne did receive him, but that no longer changed anything in the overall fate of Avar rule on the Middle Danube. The new khagan was not able to restore central power and, even though after crushing defeats he accepted Frankish overlordship and Christianity as well, he did not avert the inevitable end of Avar rule. The Slavic princes in Moravia and in the Nitra region used the Frankish victories over the Avars to strengthen their own position and ruthlessly destroyed the power of their former oppressors within their reach. As early as the beginning of the 9th century the Avars were complaining of attacks by the Slavs and the emperor was obliged to assign them new seats beyond their reach. In this period the Moravian princes probably took possession of Devín once again and began to rebuild it into one of their most important fortresses.

blocks.alt: The Devín hillfort in the 9th century according to Štefanovičová

children.text: Rastislav's Devín

The final defeat of the Avars accelerated both the state-forming and the nation-forming process of the Central European Slavs. In the territory of present-day Moravia and the part of Lower Austria north of the Danube as far as the river Kamp, the Old Moravian Principality was formed, with its probable centre at Mikulčice. In the territory of Slovakia east of the Lesser and the White Carpathians as far as the Slanské vrchy, extending into present-day Hungary as far as the Mátra, the Principality of Nitra took shape, with its centre at Nitra. Both principalities represented the initial phase of a feudal state, in which the position of the tribal prince was changing into that of a feudal sovereign and the members of the military retinues were being transformed into the nucleus of the future feudal ruling class – the nobility.

Next to the Old Moravian Principality, on the right bank of the Danube, stretched the Eastern March, the forefield of the powerful Frankish Empire, from which the successors of Charlemagne sought to control the territories of the Alpine–Carpathian area. To defend themselves against potential military incursions, the Moravian princes built mighty hillforts both in the border zone and in the interior of the country. One of the most important border hillforts of the Moravians was Devín, which protected not only the crossing of the Danube from the Eastern March but also the border against neighbouring Nitra, which had an equally strong fortress in the area of the present-day Bratislava Castle.

blocks.caption: 1. The central hillfort (the present-day castle), 3. Na Pieskach, 4. Nad Lomom
blocks.alt: 1. The central hillfort (the present-day castle), 3. Na Pieskach, 4. Nad Lomom

children.text: Devín was not merely a plain border fortress protecting access into the interior of the Old Moravian Principality from the south and the east. Given its earlier past as a former seat of local Slavic and Avar princes, it continued to be one of the principal princely strongholds. This is shown both by the form of the fortification and the occupation of the castle hill and by the building of satellite hillforts on the heights of Devínska Kobyla, which strengthened the defensive capacity of the central hillfort. The excavated hillforts at the localities known as Na pieskoch and Nad lomom, which were built during the reign of Prince Rastislav, as well as the dense occupation of the whole area of the south-western tip of present-day Slovakia and of the adjoining parts of present-day Austria, testify to the extraordinary importance of Devín in the 9th century. This is also borne out by the numerous richly furnished graves discovered either directly in the area of the present-day castle or in the wider surroundings.

Rastislav also did exceptional service in building up Devín as a princely stronghold and a fortress against the Franks, who were not at all pleased by his independent and sovereign policy. From 855, therefore, they waged almost continuous war against him with the aim of preserving the vassal dependence of Great Moravia on East Francia, which had arisen out of the eastern part of Charlemagne's empire under the Treaty of Verdun of 843. One of the many military encounters between Rastislav and the armies of the East Frankish king Louis the German took place, as I have already mentioned in the first chapter, at Devín in 864. It was probably Louis's response to the arrival of the Byzantine mission, but from the Frankish point of view it ended in failure, even though they interpreted the compromise peace as their own victory. Rastislav must have had confidence in himself and, above all, must have trusted the whole fortified complex of the Moravians at the Devín Gate when he let himself be surrounded in the hillfort by what was certainly a powerful and numerous army and did not withdraw into the interior. The defences of Devín probably looked truly formidable, since the East Frankish king did not even attempt to overcome them by force and chose a compromise agreement with a formal oath of fealty on Rastislav's part, which both of them knew would be worth nothing. The best testimony to the failure of this campaign is the fact that the Frankish annalist himself, in recording the event, noted the breaking of the oath by the Great Moravian ruler, but above all the continuation of the missionary work of Constantine and Methodius.

children.text: In the cadastral area of the village, on a promontory above the confluence of the rivers Danube and Morava, stand the remains of a medieval castle, in whose grounds older traces of fortification work have been discovered. The finds relating to Slavic occupation are of great importance. Probably as early as the 8th century a hillfort was built on the site of the present castle, making use of the remains of an older fortification (the rampart on the northern side, dug during the Roman period). From the “Annals of Fulda” we learn, under the year 864, probably about the Devín hillfort (Dowina). The hillfort occupied almost the whole area of the present medieval castle. During the reign of Prince Rastislav (846–870) the hillfort, together with the occupation around it, if it was not directly the centre of the empire, certainly belonged among the most important Great Moravian seats, which is confirmed by the written mention quoted above. Besides the great quantity of finds that confirm the written sources, there is also the tripartite church building uncovered in 1984–1985 at the locality known as “Nad prístaviskom”.
Finds

A three-apse (triconch) church building has been attested at the hillfort — the perimeter walls and the partition walls were bonded together, which proves that the whole building was erected at one time, without any later addition. On the outside the walls were covered with white lime plaster. The walls of the interior were covered with plaster decorated with paintings in earth colours (the church at Bratislava Castle and the church buildings at Mikulčice, for example, were decorated in a similar way). In its execution the building belongs to the architecture that arose in the 9th century in Great Moravia. The dating was helped by graves (6 of them survived) which lay to the south near the building and which, on the evidence of the accompanying material, were assigned to the 9th century. The chronological placing of the building was also helped by a cemetery, several graves of which overlay the walls of the church. On the basis of the accompanying material and coins, J. Eisner dated the cemetery to the 11th and the beginning of the 13th century, which suggests that burials were made in the cemetery at a time when the building had already gone out of use (was in ruins). Besides the church building with its adjoining cemetery, a densely built-up area with settlement structures was identified within the hillfort.

Settlement structures were identified across the whole area of the hillfort, with the main concentration in the north-western corner. Square ground-level cabins of log construction served as dwellings. Log cabins were identified, for example, by the northern rampart and on the eastern slope. The settlement situated within the hillfort was considerably developed in the second half of the 9th century and at the beginning of the 10th century; it may have come into being as early as the 8th century.

Equally intensive occupation has been attested outside the hillfort. Besides several smaller finds, three cemeteries in the cadastral area of the village of Devín stand out, which suggest a larger number of inhabitants than is usual for the 9th century.

The cemetery at the locality known as “Mladošovičov vinohrad” was investigated by J. Eisner. He uncovered only 12 graves here, but even so the excavation showed that the cemetery was more extensive; since it lay in an area of cultivated land, however, it was not possible to continue the excavation. One further grave was uncovered later. Despite their small number, the graves display rich furnishings. Only one grave was without finds. Besides pottery and several iron objects, the jewellery was represented above all by grape-cluster earrings. In grave no. 9 earrings were discovered, together with a necklace of glass beads with a crescent-shaped pendant.

In 1953 Ľ. Kraskovská uncovered a second cemetery at the locality known as “Staré Vinohrady”. As at the previous cemetery, only 24 graves were uncovered here as well, although this too was a more extensive burial ground. In some graves remains of a wooden construction or of wooden lining were identified. Among the graves three symbolic graves (cenotaphs) were also uncovered. The orientation of the graves was found to be inconsistent. The pottery discovered at the site was decorated not only with wavy lines but also with an incised horizontal line. A frequent find in the graves was a small iron knife. Weapons appeared in the male graves (a spear, axes of the so-called bearded type). Beside grave no. 17 a single iron spur with widened arms and a short goad was discovered (dated to the first half of the 9th century), probably belonging to a member of a warband. The female graves contained more modest furnishings, mostly simple ring earrings or earrings with a knot in the middle of the hoop.

blocks.caption: Stained-glass decoration of a church window (Harmadyová 2020)
blocks.alt: Stained-glass decoration of a church window (Harmadyová 2020)

children.text: The largest cemetery so far was uncovered at the locality known as “Za kostolom”. It was investigated in the 1960s and 1970s by I. Keller. 122 graves were uncovered here, and in some of them a wooden lining of the grave pit was identified. Almost half of the graves (40%) are children's graves. Finds were identified in only 58 graves, the greater part of them pottery and iron knives. In the female graves simple ring earrings were represented, sometimes with a knot or with ribbed bulges. Besides the simpler earrings, the grape-cluster earrings that were popular (mainly in the 9th century) were also discovered.

The marked concentration of larger sites points to the importance of the Devín area in the 9th century. Probably during the 8th century the focus of occupation shifted from Devínska Nová Ves to the Devín area. The cemeteries outside the area of the hillfort probably served the population of the settlement below the hillfort, while the cemetery by the church building within the hillfort may have served members of the magnate's retinue.

Despite the concentration of occupation at Devín, the area of Devínska Nová Ves did not remain empty. It may probably have been a “periphery”. Two hillforts built in the immediate vicinity might point to this. They were built on the western spur of Devínska Kobyla at the locality known as “Na pieskach” (Fig. 6) and at the locality known as “Nad lomom” (Fig. 7). Both were systematically investigated by Ľ. Kraskovská. They probably did not exist at the same time and it is not possible to determine which was built earlier. The hillforts probably had a defensive and a refuge function; their task was to guard the approach to Devín. The “Na pieskoch” hillfort was fortified with a grillage construction. The sloping front part of the rampart was reinforced with thick timbers. The whole construction was reinforced with dry-laid stones. A ditch was dug in front of the fortification, and the earth obtained in digging it may have been used to fill in the grillage construction. The northern part of the rampart was not reinforced with a timber construction but consisted only of an earthen bank. There was no need to build a more complex fortification here, since from the north the hillfort was protected by an inaccessible steep slope. Both hillforts were fortified in the same way. This type of fortification corresponds to Slavic hillforts of the 9th–10th century. At the “Nad lomom” hillfort two features of log construction were uncovered. In feature II 3 ovens were identified. At both hillforts traces of a fire were discovered, which probably caused their demise.”

As is clear from the article above, Devín in the time of Great Moravia cannot be understood as a single isolated hillfort, but rather as an extensive agglomeration comprising several settlements with an economic hinterland and at the same time comprising a system of at least three hillforts, which did not serve only as places of refuge: one of them undoubtedly served as the seat of a magnate (the area of the present-day castle), or even as a princely seat. That the theory of Devín's princely importance is not mere fiction is suggested by the records in the chronicles of the period, which mention Devín directly in connection with Rastislav's war against the Frankish king Louis the German. There is no need to doubt that the Dowina mentioned in the chronicle is Devín — it is precisely the extent, the strategic position and the near impregnability of the Devín hillforts that suggest themselves as an exceptionally advantageous place for organising a defence against a strong German army. Let me quote an extract from an article that deals with the records in the Annals of Fulda and the Annals of St Bertin concerning Devín and its importance for our ancestors.

blocks.text: In the month of August King Louis marched out with a great army across the Danube and besieged Rastislav in a certain town which in the tongue of that people is called Dowina. He (Rastislav), however, since he did not dare to meet the king's armies, and since he saw that he had no way by which he might escape, was forced in his straits to give as many hostages, and in such number, as the king commanded. He furthermore confirmed by oath that he, with all his (Rastislav's) magnates, would keep faith with the king for all his days, even though he had not kept it until then.

children.text: Several questions with various possible interpretations arise from this text:

I ask how it is possible that, after all the intrigues Rastislav had caused Louis — I have in mind the conclusion of alliances with Carloman (in 861) — the king was willing to let Rastislav go on ruling? After all, Rastislav and Carloman at that time invaded Bavaria with their own armies, straight into the territory of King Louis. They destroyed, burned and killed as far as the river Inn. And it was not only the association with Carloman: the whole Cyrillo-Methodian work was also beginning to take shape. How could Louis ignore these great transgressions of Rastislav's? Louis was certainly extremely well informed by his envoys and certainly knew what was happening in Great Moravia. He certainly received reports that Constantine and Methodius wanted to disrupt Latin influence in this territory. How could the East Frankish king let Rastislav go on reigning after these serious events? Well, something here does not add up for me...

The tendentiousness of the Annals of Fulda has to be taken into account. He may indeed have besieged Rastislav, but he was not able to humble him — the passage about the impossibility of escaping from the town may be invented. The same goes for not daring to meet the king's armies — rather the opposite: it was Louis who did not dare to storm the place and needlessly shed the blood of many soldiers. When the king saw that he could not humble Rastislav, he decided to negotiate with him. The straits that are mentioned, however, could be taken into account from a geographical point of view. Devín lies in terrain that is hard to reach, with the Great Moravian acropolis right on the steep Devín castle hill. The uncovered ground plan of the church suggests that it either had a room serving as a baptistery or a room for secular, ruling purposes. And even if it had no secular living quarters, part of the acropolis no longer exists today — the part where a secular building, Rastislav's, may have stood during the siege of Dowina.

blocks.text: Louis, king of Germany, marched out with an army against the Bulgarian khagan by the name of (...), who had promised that he would become a Christian; from there he intended to set out in order to establish the march of the Wends, if he should see that success would be granted to him.

children.text: Success, however, was not granted to him. Nor did he establish the march. From the Annals of Fulda it does indeed appear that Rastislav promised the king obedience, but that obedience was not only formal — it was also not kept. Today, though, we can compare the sources and find out whether the Annals of Fulda were right. The march of the Wends (the Moravian Slavs) could not be established. Other annals, those of Xanten, do mention under the year 869 that Louis ruled in the east over the Slavs, in Bavaria, Alamannia, Churrhaetia, Saxony, Swabia and Thuringia. They might be proof that Rastislav really did submit. But why then do they style the subject ruler Rastislav as “rex”??? — Rasticius rex Margorum. Another source — the Deeds of the Frankish Kings — says under the year 865 that Louis the German gave Carloman Noricum, that is Bavaria, and the marches against the Wends — Carloman did not have a march of the Wends (the Slavs), only marches which were supposed to win them for him.

And that is important — the Annals of Fulda are misleading under the year 864. Dowina did not surrender, Rastislav's territory was not subjugated. Indeed, a year after the campaign against Dowina we have a direct report of the inviolability of the territory of the Moravian Slavs. And in the same way the Annals of Xanten meant to lead us down the wrong path. They mention the march of the Wends, yet at the same time they contradict themselves and style Rastislav a king and his dominion a kingdom — regnum. In the 9th century, after all, regna were independent territories. That is why, for example, Svatopluk's Nitra — regnum Zuentibaldi — is also mentioned as a regnum, because in the last years of Rastislav's reign it was practically autonomous. It must also be added that it is mistaken to think that the regna of the 9th century are the same kind of kingdoms as the Hungarian, Polish and Bohemian kingdoms two or three centuries later (Ďurica 1997, Zrubec 1991, Irša 2008).

And these are important matters. As can be seen, the Frankish annalists tried at all costs to turn the victory to their own side. But thanks to a few of them we can prove that this cannot always have been so. Dowina, that is Devín, was a genuine centre, an agglomeration stretching from Devínska Nová Ves across the Moravské pole (the Marchfeld) to Carnuntum, to present-day Bratislava, with its centre on the Devín castle rock. Archaeology and a correct interpretation of the written sources are able to prove it. The advantageously placed hillforts proved by archaeologists and the rock at the confluence of the Danube and the Morava, hard to take, greatly helped the decision not to storm Devín. In order to sweep the failure of their own side under the carpet, the Annals of Fulda turned this failure onto Rastislav's side — he supposedly had nowhere to flee in his straits and therefore submitted. It was rather Louis, hemmed in by the rivers Morava and Danube, by their marshes and branches, and also by Devínska Kobyla with its guard hillforts, who was unsuccessful.
On the basis of these facts I consider the area of present-day Devín to be an agglomeration of the “civis Dowina” type.”
Na Pieskách:

Access to the hillfort is easy: a green marked trail leads from Devínska Nová Ves, from Pod Lipovým street, and after a 10-minute walk it brings you to the top of the hillfort. What I consider an incomprehensible and inexcusable act of neglect, however, is that
no signpost gives any warning
that the trail runs across a hillfort. It is also very sad that in the area of the hillfort
you will not find even a mention of the fact that you are standing on a Great Moravian hillfort!

children.text: Access:

Even easier than to the Na Pieskách hillfort. A yellow marked trail (or a blue one from the other side) will take you to Sandberg, with those amazing sand formations, which contain a great quantity of fossils, on your left hand, while on your right hand is the hill that juts out above the road and above the river Morava — that is the Nad Lomom hillfort. On the top of the hillfort hill there is an ugly building belonging to the waterworks company — they really could not have chosen a better place to build it under socialism. I must express my praise for the new information panel lying between the two hillforts. It even includes a 3D model of the Lom hillfort, which is evidently unique in our conditions.
